title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing — October 1, 2026 (Six Scores Meet Their First Real Evidence, One Gets a Re-Check)
headline: Six scores had never been measured before tonight; the proposed changes are not yet applied.
summary:
Nothing in this briefing has been applied. Every score named as published is the live score. Every other number is a proposal.

The night's main finding is about the benchmark's own starting values. Six of the seven proposals are first-ever measurements. Valencia, Madrid, the University of Glasgow, Cornell University, Vietnam and the University of Birmingham had never been checked against evidence. Each proposal reads lower than its published score, by 3.6 to 19.0 points. That gap reflects a first full assessment, not a measured decline in conduct.

Valencia (published 60.9, proposed 41.9) and Madrid (published 65.6, proposed 48.1) are scored on city-government conduct only. Both cities earned credit for recent action. Glasgow, ranked first of 100 universities at 62.5, is proposed at 48.7 with low confidence, because the adverse sources are news reports. Cornell (54.7, proposed 41.9) is scored on the New York Attorney General's review and its own statement, not on lawsuit allegations. Birmingham (43.0, proposed 39.4) would sit 0.6 points below a band line. Vietnam (34.4, proposed 23.8) is scored on confirmed detentions, not an alleged abduction.

Bangladesh is the one real re-check. Its published 39.8 and a proposed 33.1 reflect three September laws that strip the human rights commission of power over enforced disappearances.

Three published readings held: Egypt (21.9), Delta Air Lines (62.5) and Tennessee (30.0). Spain and South Africa were measured but not filed. Fifteen more entities were screened, including five at or near the lowest score.

Release watch: 0 sources registered — detection did not run.

pipeline.rosterNote: The roster held at 1,329 entities. The lookback window ran 2026-09-17 to 2026-10-01 (14 days).
pipeline.queueHandling: Twenty-seven organizations were reviewed. Seven proposed changes were filed, six of them first-ever measurements. Two readings were measured and not filed, three were confirmed, and fifteen were screened without a full score. Nothing was applied.

topSignals.title: Valencia's 60.9 Was a Starting Value; Its First Real Check Proposes 41.9
topSignals.whyItMatters: Valencia's published 60.9 came from a template number, not research. A first evidence-based reading proposes 41.9. The city's flood response earned credit. Its homelessness record did not.
topSignals.description:
Valencia is ranked 39th among global cities with a published score of 60.9 out of 100. That number was never checked against evidence. A first full assessment proposes 41.9, which would move Valencia from the Established band to the Functional band. The published score is unchanged, and the proposal has not been applied.

This is a first measurement, not a measured decline in conduct. The assessment scores only the city government, the Ajuntament de València. The regional government's conduct, including its flood alert that critics called late, is excluded.

In the 15 to 17 September 2026 flood episode the city acted early. It activated its orange-alert protocols before the rain began, suspended activity at 26 centres in flood-prone zones, and handled 250 fire incidents and 211 police calls. Those actions earn the top rating the benchmark gives for anticipating harm and responding to it.

The weaker side is homelessness. On 1 October 2026 opposition parties said the city refused to run an official homeless census, and that shelter capacity is 57, 20 and 10 places. Those are opposition statements, not findings, and the assessment weighs them that way.

evidence.quote: Los Bomberos atendieron 250 incidencias (en su mayoría de carácter menor, relacionadas con achiques, caída de ramas y saneamientos)
evidence.claim: The city activated orange-alert protocols before the episode began, suspended activity at 26 centres in flood-prone zones, and handled 250 fire incidents and 211 police calls.

evidence.quote: el Ayuntamiento se ha negado a hacer un censo oficial de las personas sin techo
evidence.claim: Opposition parties state the city refused an official homeless census and that shelter capacity (57, 20, 10 places) is insufficient; a city count at one settlement rose from 21 (2022) to 114 (2025).
evidence.source: Viva Valencia — opposition demands shelter for homeless people under red alert

evidence.claim: After a regional court annulled the 2024 moratorium, the city enacted a 2% per-neighbourhood cap on tourist flats in May 2026, described as Spain's most restrictive.

topSignals.title: Madrid's 65.6 Was Never Measured; a First Check Proposes 48.1
topSignals.whyItMatters: Madrid's city hall helped an evicted 87-year-old woman return home within a week and counts its homeless every year. Its published 65.6 still outran the evidence. A first check proposes 48.1.
topSignals.description:
Madrid's published score is 65.6 out of 100, in the Established band. It had never been individually assessed. A first full assessment proposes 48.1, in the Functional band. Confidence is low: 20 of the 40 sub-measures have no evidence and sit at the default midpoint of 3 out of 5. The published score is unchanged, and nothing has been applied.

The city's recent conduct was good. On 23 September 2026 Mayor José Luis Martínez-Almeida offered an evicted 87-year-old woman immediate housing. The city's housing company then mediated an agreement that returned her home by 29 September. Madrid also counts homelessness every year: 1,015 people were sleeping rough in 2025, down 9%.

The weight on the other side is Cañada Real, a settlement on Madrid's edge. About 4,500 people, at least 1,800 of them children, have lived without electricity since October 2020. In 2025 the European Committee of Social Rights found Spain in violation of the European Social Charter. Responsibility is shared among the national government, the region and the city, so the assessment scores the city's share with low confidence.

evidence.quote: Ayer entendieron que el Ayuntamiento era el instrumento adecuado para poder llegar a un acuerdo
evidence.claim: The city's housing company mediated the agreement returning the evicted woman home (countervailing, credited).

evidence.quote: The electricity supply was interrupted in October 2020 until today.
evidence.claim: The ECSR found Spain violated the European Social Charter over Cañada Real power cuts affecting about 4,500 people.
evidence.source: FEANTSA (reporting European Committee of Social Rights decision)

topSignals.title: Glasgow, Ranked First of 100 Universities, Had Never Been Measured
topSignals.whyItMatters: The index's top-ranked university leads on repairing its slavery past, and overrode its own staff and students on arms. A first check proposes 48.7, but the adverse sources are news reports, not court or government records.
topSignals.description:
The University of Glasgow is ranked first among 100 universities at 62.5 out of 100, in the Established band. That score was never assessed against evidence. A first assessment proposes 48.7, in the Functional band, a 13.8-point gap. Confidence is low. The published score is unchanged, and the proposal has not been applied.

Glasgow's record on repairing historical harm is the strongest the benchmark has seen in a university. It published a report on its own profits from slavery in 2018 and runs a joint reparative-justice master's degree with the University of the West Indies. Its Top-Up programme targets students from deprived areas, care-experienced students, refugees and young carers.

On current conduct the record is weaker. In November 2024 the University Court voted 14 to 7 against arms divestment, after its own consultation found 81% of staff and 86% of students in favour. Emails reported by Al Jazeera on 24 September 2026 show Glasgow told BAE Systems, a funder, that it had informed Police Scotland of a planned student protest at a 2023 careers fair. In June 2026 it opened a voluntary severance scheme over a forecast shortfall of about GBP 10 million.

The proposed band crossing rests on news reports and student press. No court, government or international-body source was located, so the assessment holds this finding at low confidence.

evidence.quote: Meanwhile, emails show the University of Glasgow apparently reassured BAE it had informed Police Scotland of a planned protest targeting an October 2023 careers fair.
evidence.claim: Glasgow coordinated with a funder over student protest.

evidence.quote: Academic freedom is undermined while arms companies hold such influence over what gets researched, funded, and legitimised on campus.
evidence.claim: Arms companies were invited to sit on a Glasgow University advisory committee, according to Declassified UK research reported by The Tab.

topSignals.title: Cornell's 54.7 Meets Its First Evidence: A State Review and Faculty Criticism
topSignals.whyItMatters: Cornell's score had never been checked. The proposed 41.9 rests on a state review, the university's own statement and a faculty finding. Lawsuit allegations are not scored as fact.
topSignals.description:
Cornell University is ranked 12th among 100 universities at 54.7 out of 100, in the Functional band. A first assessment proposes 41.9, also Functional, so no band change would result. The published score is unchanged, and the proposal has not been applied.

The New York State Attorney General announced a review of Cornell's initial response to a 2024 sexual-assault allegation, and the Tompkins County District Attorney reopened the criminal case (Boston Globe, 30 September 2026). Cornell's 21 September 2026 statement calls the allegations deeply disturbing but acknowledges no failure and routes the response to the legal process. The assessment scores those actions. It does not treat the lawsuit's allegations as established fact.

Separately, Cornell's Faculty Senate found in November 2025 that temporary suspensions were used to deter, retaliate or compel compliance, and that about 85% of suspended students had taken part in protest. On the credit side, Cornell's need-based aid covers the full cost of attendance for families earning up to $75,000, and a March 2026 task force adopted evidence-based prevention programmes.

evidence.quote: The New York state attorney general announced a review of the university's initial response to the allegations.
evidence.claim: The NY Attorney General is reviewing Cornell's handling.

evidence.quote: Cornell University is aware of a lawsuit concerning the deeply disturbing allegations of sexual assault involving members of the student community that occurred in 2024.
evidence.claim: Cornell's institutional response to the lawsuit.

evidence.quote: coercive discipline used to deter, retaliate, or compel immediate compliance with Cornell policies
evidence.claim: Faculty Senate criticism of temporary suspensions of protesters.

evidence.quote: Students from families earning up to $75,000 receive grants, scholarships and work-study that cover the full cost of attendance.
evidence.claim: Countervailing: need-based aid framework.

topSignals.title: Vietnam's 34.4 Was a Starting Value; a First Check Proposes 23.8
topSignals.whyItMatters: Vietnam's published score was never checked. State media confirmed two Viet Tan activists were detained, and the group says they were abducted from Cambodia. The assessment scores the confirmed detention, not the abduction claim.
topSignals.description:
Vietnam is ranked 106th among countries at 34.4 out of 100, in the Developing band. It had never been individually assessed. A first assessment proposes 23.8, still Developing. The published score is unchanged, and the proposal has not been applied.

On 29 September 2026 ABC News reported that Vietnamese state media confirmed the detention of Australian Hiep Tran and Norwegian-Vietnamese Duc Thuan Nguyen. Their group, Viet Tan, alleges both were abducted in Cambodia and taken across the border. The abduction is an allegation and is not scored as fact. The detention is.

The assessment also weighs Human Rights Watch's 2026 World Report: more than 160 political prisoners in 2025 and at least 32 convictions under Article 331 of the penal code. On the credit side, Vietnam abolished the death penalty for eight offences in June 2025 and set 2026 and 2030 targets in a health-care roadmap. Fourteen of the 40 sub-measures rest on default scores, so confidence is medium, not high.

evidence.quote: were abducted in Cambodia, then forcibly taken across the border
evidence.claim: Viet Tan alleges two of its members were abducted in Cambodia and taken into Vietnam; Vietnamese state media reported their detention.
Vietnam held over 160 political prisoners in 2025 and arrested at least 40 others for criticising the government.
OHCHR welcomed Vietnam's abolition of the death penalty for eight offences (countervailing).

topSignals.title: Bangladesh Is the Night's One Real Re-Check: Three September Laws Weighed
topSignals.whyItMatters: Unlike the first-baseline cases, Bangladesh already had a real measurement. Three September 2026 laws strip the human rights commission of power over enforced disappearances, and a proposed 33.1 reflects them.
topSignals.description:
Bangladesh's published score is 39.8 out of 100, in the Developing band. It was set on 16 June 2026 after labour reforms. A re-check proposes 33.1, still Developing. The published score is unchanged, and the proposal has not been applied.

Human Rights Watch reported on 22 September 2026 that three laws passed in September remove the National Human Rights Commission's power to investigate enforced disappearances, and move the Rapid Action Battalion's personnel and powers to a new unit with fewer safeguards. HRW says the laws break the governing party's reform commitments.

Of the 6.7-point gap, 4.8 points were measured on 21 September 2026 and were too small to file on their own. The other 1.9 points come from the new laws. The June labour-reform credit is kept. Confidence is medium: the evidence on the new laws is a single watchdog source, but the laws themselves are public acts of parliament.

evidence.quote: Three laws approved in September 2026 by the Bangladeshi parliament have reversed human rights protections and broken the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party's (BNP) commitments to reform.
evidence.claim: September 2026 laws reverse interim-era rights protections.

evidence.quote: The new government's efforts to shield security forces from scrutiny and accountability offer no reason to trust that killings and disappearances will remain a thing of the past.
evidence.claim: The laws shield security forces from accountability.

boundaryWatch.trigger: A court, regulator or government record on the redundancy round's withheld equality impact assessment would raise the evidence quality behind the crossing.
boundaryWatch.note: Published at 43.0 in the Functional band. A first assessment lands at 39.4, 0.6 points below the Developing line, on news reports that every staff member at risk in the latest redundancy round is migrant or minority-ethnic.

boundaryWatch.trigger: A further arrest or sentence of journalists, or the closure of another independent outlet, would test the room left above the Critical line.
boundaryWatch.note: Egypt's published 21.9 sits 1.9 points above the Critical line at 20. Tonight's reading is 21.3, still Developing, after six journalists were arrested on 28 and 29 September 2026.

boundaryWatch.trigger: Evidence that Barrick has carried out the Loulo-Gounkoto agreement on overtime pay, expense reimbursement and earlier labour agreements would bear on the Critical line.
boundaryWatch.note: Barrick sits 1.2 points below the Developing line. Its 21 September 2026 collective agreement with Loulo-Gounkoto unions averted a strike, and even the most generous reading of it reaches 20.0, which is still Critical.

boundaryWatch.trigger: Final court approval of the $78.7 million fuel-dump settlement, or any admission of fault by Delta, would bear on its Harm Acknowledgment reading.
boundaryWatch.note: Delta's published 62.5 and tonight's 61.3 both sit in the Established band, 1.3 points above the Functional line at 60. The company still denies wrongdoing over the January 2020 fuel dump.

emergingRisks.risk: Published scores that were never measured may sit well above what a first reading of the evidence supports.
emergingRisks.detail: In three proposal cycles, 12 first baselines have produced 11 lower readings and one higher one. A first baseline starts every sub-measure without evidence at the default midpoint of 3 out of 5, about 50 of 100, so a starting value above that has to be earned by evidence. Many rows have not yet had a first reading.

emergingRisks.risk: The top of the universities index rests on scores that were never assessed against evidence.
emergingRisks.detail: Glasgow (rank 1), Cornell (rank 12) and Birmingham each read lower on a first baseline, and Columbia did so on 22 September. The index has three Established-band universities; Glasgow is one of them.

emergingRisks.risk: Spain's two emergency housing decrees need a parliamentary vote within 30 days, and that vote bears on Spain's housing record.
emergingRisks.detail: The Council of Ministers approved both Royal Decree-laws on 29 September 2026. They extend eviction protection to 2030. The country score already counts the action, so a failed vote would matter more than a passed one.

emergingRisks.risk: Florida's attorney general has asked a court to pause new OpenAI model development and bar minors from ChatGPT; no court has ruled.
emergingRisks.detail: The 28 September 2026 filing is an allegation, not a finding. The minor-safety concerns behind it were already scored in OpenAI's 20 September assessment. A ruling on the injunction would be the first court action.

emergingRisks.risk: Egypt, Iran and Hong Kong each recorded new press-freedom arrests or sentences within four days, in measures already at or near the lowest score.
emergingRisks.detail: Egypt arrested six journalists on 28 and 29 September, Iran sentenced journalist Abbas Abdi on 27 September, and Hong Kong arrested Boom News founder Tang Ho-wing on 30 September. Only Egypt's Transparency measure had room to move.

sectorAlerts.sector: Global Cities — Two Spanish Cities Meet Their First Real Evidence
sectorAlerts.headline: Valencia and Madrid both read about 18 points below never-assessed starting values on city-government evidence alone.
observations: Valencia: published 60.9, proposed 41.9. The city's flood protocols are credited; the regional government's flood alert is excluded.
Madrid: published 65.6, proposed 48.1, at low confidence. The city's housing help for an evicted 87-year-old is credited; Cañada Real's power cuts are scored with shared responsibility.
Spain's own country score is separate: 51.2 measured this cycle, within 0.6 points of a proposal already pending at 50.6.
New York City appears in two indexes with different published scores: 48.4 in global cities (never assessed) and 56.3 in US cities (assessed 10 June 2026).

sectorAlerts.sector: Universities — Top Ranks Meet First Evidence
sectorAlerts.headline: Three universities each read lower on a first baseline; the two highest-ranked cross a band line only on lower-quality sourcing or not at all.
observations: University of Glasgow (rank 1): published 62.5, proposed 48.7 at low confidence.
Cornell University (rank 12): published 54.7, proposed 41.9; both in the Functional band.
University of Birmingham (rank 69): published 43.0, proposed 39.4, 0.6 points below the Developing line.
Northwestern University held at 42.2: a national report released on 23 September 2026 repeats conduct the benchmark scored in July and August.

sectorAlerts.sector: Countries — Two Baselines and a Floor That Cannot Fall Further
sectorAlerts.headline: Vietnam and Bangladesh were re-read; Myanmar, Somalia, Iran and Pakistan show conduct in measures already at the lowest score.
observations: Vietnam: published 34.4, proposed 23.8. Laos (14.1) has never been assessed and Cambodia sits at 12.5, so a regional re-baseline would put the three on one footing.
Myanmar stays at 0.0: a 28 September 2026 airstrike on a market in Kyauktaw killed at least 33 people, according to Al Jazeera.
Somalia stays at 4.7: the UN humanitarian coordinator warned on 28 September 2026 about displacement and child malnutrition in Baidoa.

sectorAlerts.sector: Fortune 500 — Court Outcomes Arrive Before Admissions
sectorAlerts.headline: Delta's settlement and Meta's jury verdict each show repair or a court finding without an admission of fault.
observations: Delta Air Lines: a $78.7 million fuel-dump settlement was tentatively approved on 28 September 2026 while Delta denies wrongdoing; the reading is 61.3 against a published 62.5.
Meta Platforms stays at 7.8: a Santa Fe jury found on 25 September 2026 that Facebook deceived users about privacy, and the penalty phase is pending.
Barrick Gold stays at 18.8: a 21 September 2026 collective agreement averted a strike, but it is routine and does not reach the next band.

sectorAlerts.sector: AI Labs — Legal Pressure Is Still Allegation
sectorAlerts.headline: Florida, California and Congress each acted against AI developers in the past two weeks; no court has ruled on the OpenAI filing.
observations: Florida's attorney general sought a temporary injunction against OpenAI on 28 September 2026.
California signed SB 947 on 30 September 2026, limiting automated firing and discipline.
OpenAI stays at a published 22.5; the assessment on 20 September 2026 measured 25.0 and already scores the minor-safety concerns.

methodologyNotes.name: A First Measurement Is Not a Decline
methodologyNotes.description: Six of tonight's seven proposals are first measurements: Valencia, Madrid, the University of Glasgow, Cornell University, Vietnam and the University of Birmingham had never been checked against evidence. Their published scores were starting values, not earlier research findings. A first reading describes what the benchmark did not yet know, not what the institution did differently this week. Bangladesh is the one re-check against a real earlier baseline.

methodologyNotes.name: Allegations Are Not Scored as Facts
methodologyNotes.description: Cornell's lawsuit allegations, Vietnam's abduction claim and Florida's motion against OpenAI are allegations. The benchmark scores what an institution itself did or confirmed: Cornell's statement and the attorney general's review, Vietnam's confirmed detentions, and nothing yet for OpenAI because no court has ruled.

methodologyNotes.name: Source Quality Gates Band Crossings
methodologyNotes.description: A proposal that crosses a band line needs at least one strong source, such as a court, government or international body. Madrid and Valencia clear that bar. Glasgow and Birmingham rest on news reports and student press, so their crossings are proposed at low confidence.

methodologyNotes.name: Calibration Is Decided Once, Not One Entity at a Time
methodologyNotes.description: South Africa measured 8.7 points below its published 50.0, but most of that gap re-reads evidence the May baseline already weighed, so no proposal was filed. Spain measured within 0.6 points of a proposal already pending, so a duplicate was not filed either.

methodologyNotes.name: We Score Who Caused the Harm
methodologyNotes.description: Valencia's regional flood alert, Kingston's national police killing and the alleged abduction on Cambodian soil each belong to a different institution. The benchmark scores the Ajuntament de València, Jamaica and Vietnam, not the city or country where the event took place.
